title: The name Waheguru
hookLine: the name used by the Bhatts in their verses praising the Gurus (Swayye, ang 1402)

cards: Wah. A sound people make without deciding to. A sunset over the fields.
A baby's first step. A friend's voice on the phone after years. Now set that sound right in front of the word Guru.
Waheguru. It was the very first word on this path, back on day one.
It's the name Sikhs repeat in simran, the word in the greeting Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki fateh, the name a congregation says together as a reading ends.

teach.h: THE BHATTS: BARDS IN THE GRANTH.
teach.b: Close to the end of the Guru Granth Sahib come the Swayye of the Bhatts, verses by bards who praised the Gurus.
Tradition remembers them as poets who came to the Guru's court and sang what they saw, and their verses sit in the same scripture as the Gurus' own hymns.
Around Ang fourteen hundred and two, in a verse praising Guru Ram Das, a Bhatt named Gayand breaks again and again into one cry: Waheguru, Waheguru, Waheguru.
It reads less like a definition than like someone who can't stop saying it.
Sikhs explain the name as wonder joined to Guru: wah, the cry of astonishment, and Guru, the one who brings light and teaching. Something like wonderful Lord. Notice what kind of name that is.
Yesterday, Guru Arjan said our names describe God's deeds. Waheguru doesn't describe a deed. It describes what happens to the one who notices.

teach.h: FROM A BARD'S SONG TO DAILY SIMRAN.
teach.b: From a bard's song it became the center of daily life. Sikhs repeat it in simran, slowly or quickly, aloud or under the breath, and call it gurmantar, the Guru's own word to repeat.
A name that began as praise is now said in kitchens, cars and hospital rooms.

how: Sikhs repeat Waheguru in simran, alone or together, and use it in the greeting Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki fateh; congregations often say it aloud at the end of a reading.

o: wonder joined to Guru: something like wonderful Lord
the name of the first Guru's own teacher
a Persian title meaning king of the whole world

games.q: inside the name: tap the pairs.

s: Waheguru appears in the Granth in the Bhatts' verses
near the end of the book, in the Swayye praising the Gurus.
Waheguru is a name describing one of God's deeds
it's mostly a gasp: wonder joined to Guru.
the Bhatts' verses are kept outside the Granth
they sit in the same scripture as the Gurus' hymns.

games.q: you're a poet at the Guru's court, asked to praise what you've seen, and every careful word falls short. what do you do?
o: find the most exact title you can.
let the praise become wonder itself: Waheguru.
games.why: Bhatt Gayand cries Waheguru again and again; the name reads like someone who can't stop saying it.

practice: On each out-breath, let the name come at walking pace: wah, then he, then guru, and let the pause after it stretch too. If you'd rather not say it, say just wah, the sound of wonder, for one thing today that deserves it.
When your mind runs off, the next wah brings it back.

wordCard.voice: The name Waheguru. Wonder joined to Guru: the name the Bhatts cried out in their verses, and the name Sikhs repeat in simran today. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: Waheguru, wonder joined to Guru, the name Sikhs repeat in simran.

carryVoice: Your line: wonderful lord. Wonder comes first, and the Guru with it. Go gently.

sources.ref: Ang 1402–1403 (Swayye of Bhatt Gayand, in praise of Guru Ram Das)
